The statement was made that
there is a very material difference between the subject matter of this motion and the subject matter of the bill presented by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). I looked into the question rather carefully, and I can see very little difference. It seems to me that if the bill presented by the hon. member for New Westminster were to pass there would be nothing left to debate on the subject matter of this motion. I think that the mover will agree that the question to be discussed here is that of the domestic rates on grain moving westward. As far as the interprovincial movement is concerned, it does not seem to me that there is anything to engage particularly the attention of the house. The export rate on grain to Fort William from any point is known; it is the Crowsnest rate. So far as grain moving between the provinces in that direction is concerned the^rate is in no case higher than the Fort William rate. So that I think when boiled down it simply means that whereas the hon. member for New Westminster moved that the domestic rate on 
grain moving westward be equalized with the export rate, this motion provides that the rate on grain moving westward shall be set three cents higher than the export rate. It seems to me that these bills very closely duplicate each other, and that the ruling of Mr. Speaker as first given is entirely correct.

subtopic: DEBATE AND RULING OP MR. SPEAKER ON POINT OP ORDER RAISED BY MR. POWER ON THURSDAY, FEBRUARY 20

Mr. Speaker, if this
were a matter of legal argument one might understand the observations of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Howe), but it is a question of reading words. All that is necessary is to read the bill and' the resolution. I shall take the bill first. It deals with traffic "moving westwardly from Fort William, and from all points on all lines of railway west of Fort William, to Vancouver, British Columbia and to ports on the Pacific coast." It deals specifically with traffic from Fort William, or points on all lines of railway west of Fort William, to Vancouver, British Columbia, and to all ports on the Pacific coast. The resolution deals with an entirely separate and distinct matter. H the minister would only take the trouble to read the resolution he would not have been guilty of making the observations he has made this afternoon, because he will find that there is no similarity between them at all, and not a scintilla of evidence to support that view. Let us look at the resolution:	"That, in the opinion
of this house, the domestic freight rate on grain and grain products moving from any point"-not Fort William-"in the provinces of"-not Ontario; not Fort William, but "Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia"-that is, traffic moving from those four provinces westward-"to a point"-not Vancouver or Pacific points-"in any of the said provinces,"-that is interprovincial trade -"or from any point, to another point, in any of the said provinces," be adjusted or reduced to at least not more than three cents differential. Now, all one has to do is to read, and I am sure if that is read by the Minister of Railways he will not suggest that these two things are the same.

The bill of the hon. member for New Westminster seeks to enlarge the original legislation so that it will encompass the British Columbia coast. At the same time, as I read the bill it would apply just as well to all lines in the prairie provinces. The bill may not be

subtopic: DEBATE AND RULING OP MR. SPEAKER ON POINT OP ORDER RAISED BY MR. POWER ON THURSDAY, FEBRUARY 20
speechtext:
On Thursday I began to give a decision in this matter which, to-day, I shall complete as follows:
The adjournment of the debate last Thursday on the second reading of Bill No. 2, am act. to amend the Railway Act (rates on grain), meant that the question shall again be considered at a future sitting when the order for public bills will be reached. This is what is called, in parliamentary procedure, appointing a matter for consideration by the house. May, page 272, gives many precedents showing that the discussion of an appointed matter cannot be anticipated by a motion. The bill proposes to extend to the westward traffic, from Fort William to Vancouver and the Pacific coast, the rates on grain and flour agreed to in the Orowsnest pass agreement embodied in its essence as follows in the annual statutes of 1897:
That there shall be a reduction in the company's present rates and tolls on grain and flour from all points on its main line, branches or connections west of Fort William to Fort William and Port Arthur and all points east, of three cents per one hundred pounds.
The order adjourning the debate had been passed by the house when Mr. Perley, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, moved that domestic freight rates on grain products, from and to any point in the province of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, be reduced to at least not more than three cents per hundred pounds over the existing export rates.
There is sufficient similarity in the bill and the motion to confine them to one debate. The domestic rates dealt with in the motion are included in the rates and tolls on grain and flour mentioned in the Orowsnest agreement. The question centralizes on grain rates in western Canada, and debate thereon could not be allowed last Thursday a few minutes after the house had adjourned it to a future sitting. The difference in details between the two propositions may be dealt with by moving amendments when the bill is in committee of the whole, but it is not
	.
sufficient to justify a duplication of the debate. It is a well known principle that the same question cannot be raised twice in the same session.
The main object sought both by the bill and the motion is the reduction of rates on grain and its products moving westwardly in the prairie provinces and British Columbia. They are both intended to put an end to an alleged unfairness in the present rates, and the whole debate, which will be centred on that grievance, must take place on the bill and not on the motion.
As Campion says, in applying the anticipation rule, preference is given to the discussion which leads to the most effective results, and this has established a descending scale. A bill has the right of way and cannot be sidetracked by a motion.
I cannot follow any other course than to decide that the discussion of Mr. Perley's motion is blocked by the adjournment of the debate on Bill No. 2, and for that reason, I have to declare that the motion cannot now be debated and must be struck off the order paper.
This decision does not prevent the subject matter of Mr. Perley's motion from being discussed when the bill is under discussion.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OP ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext:
Whereas, the concentration of economic power in the hands of a comparatively small and irresponsible group has failed to provide security and a decent standard of living for large numbers of our people;
Therefore be it resolved, that; in the opinion of this house, industrial, commercial and financial organizations and undertakings that are failing to function in the general interest should be taken over by the appropriate public authorities and operated as public services or cooperative enterprises.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OP ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext:
Speaking to the resolution, for several years I have introduced a resolution urging a new economic and social set-up, which I have called the cooperative commonwealth, and the need for it is more pressing to-day than ever, especially in view of the disturbed international situation. Again, we have a new house and many of the members have not heard the point of view of our group.
Last year I was able to summon the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), then Prime Minister, as my star witness to the failure of capitalism, and had the legislation of his government implemented the promises of his earlier radio addresses the situation in the house and throughout the country might have been very different to-day. This year I propose to use rather freely the report of the royal commission on price spreads, and although my friend from East Kootenay (Mr. Stevens) did not see his way to second this resolution I gladly accord him recognition of the great benefit he conferred upon the country by taking the initiative in urging that investigation. The present government, of course, is not responsible for the report. Several of the Liberal members of the committee made reservations, one wrote a dissenting report. However, I would point out that the government is decidedly responsible for solving the problems revealed by the report and by the evidence.
That economic power is concentrated in the hands of a comparatively small group is generally conceded, except perhaps by the members of that group. I should like to call attention to a very fine case put forward in a recent book called Social Planning for Canada, with particular reference to the chapter dealing with the structure of Canadian industry. I quote:
There were once more than forty banks in Canada. There are now ten. Of these, the three largest do 70 per cent of the business. The four largest 80 per cent and, though they compete strenuously in service, they present a united front on interest rates.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OP ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext:
I am referring to
a book entitled Social Planning for Canada, published by the research committee of the
444	COMMONS
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Woodsworth	.
League for Social Reconstruction. I am glad the hon. member gave me an opportunity to state the authorship of this book. The price spreads report states at pages 25 and 26 that of the non-financial corporations, the total assets of 100 of the largest companies increased during the period 1923 to 1933 from $5,095,651,000 to $7,324,323,000, or 43-7 per cent. Excluding five transportation companies, the increase was 83-6 per cent. Then, as I have tried to point out from time to time in this house, we have a system of interlocking directorates. As one writer puts it, our business leaders spread their tentacles over every phase of human life. We are born in their hospitals, we are buried in their cemeteries. In the interval it is they who decide what we shall eat, what we shall drink, what we shall wear, what we shall see, what we shall hear and what we shall smoke.
In my resolution I state that this oligarchy is irresponsible. I do not use that word to mean that it is crazy, although it often acts in a way which in my judgment would show that it is in reality blind to its own ultimate interests. I use the word in the sense that it is not responsible to any duly constituted authority. Industry to-day is self governed. Let me quote from page 13 of the price spreads report, as follows:
It has shown-
Referring to the evidence-
-that a few great corporations are predominant in the industries that have been investigated; also that this power, all the more dangerous because it is impersonal, can be wielded in such a way that competition within the industry is blocked, the welfare of the producer disregarded, and the interests of the investor ignored.
And again:
-the corporate form of business, not only often gives freedom from legal liability, but also facilitates the evasion of moral responsibility for inequitable and uneconomic practices.
I think we are all aware, as is stated in the report, that to a large extent the greatest expansion in our corporations has occurred during this present century. With regard to the ownership and control of corporations the report states that the development of the corporation with its multiple shareholders has made it possible for an individual to own without controlling, and to control without owning. This means that control over the physical assets of the instruments of production and distribution is passing from the property owner to the managerial groups. This is altogether a new and rather menacing development in our industrial, commercial and financial life. The report then goes on to show the various methods by which this condition has been arrived at. We have the

minority control attained by means of the proxy system. Every hon. member knows that at annual meetings it is next to impossible for a small shareholder to obtain any redress or even to get information which it may be necessary he should have. One very significant statement in the report is that very few directors own more than one per cent of the voting stock of the companies they direct. We talk about democracy in politics, but I submit that there is an absolute negation of democracy in our industrial life when only a few directors have any great stock ownership in the companies which they control. The report summarizes the various devices by which minority control is maintained. I should like to quote from the report very briefly in order to bring the whole picture before the house. There is the holding company which owns a controlling interest in the voting securities and in this connection the report reads:
The holding company may also be used to recapitalize the financial structure of one or more enterprises through a substitution of its securities for securities of subsidiary companies.
The report states that almost invariably this is a form of stock watering. It states that the holding company may also be used to pyramid the voting control to give its organizers, with a minimum amount of investment, control over the subsidiary. Without going into the matter in too great detail, I might mention also the devices of non-voting stock and the voting trust. The report concludes by stating:
These facts support the view that the real motive of many consolidations was financial gain to the professional promoter and investment dealer.
And again:
In general, the refinancing schemes were so constructed as to afford the public the privilege of subscribing the requisite amount of cash while endowing the promoters with unhampered control of the new companies.
The whole matter is summarized in these words:
This summary of earnings histories points to the following conclusions:-
(1)	That the refinancing operations were attended' by gross over-valuation of assets and consequent over-capitalization.
(2)	That the so-called bonds, preferred shares and class "A" shares had in many instances no real equity junior to them; in other words, that the receivers of the common stock gave no real consideration to the company for the issue of these shares.
Certain references to corporate practices were made in the evidence but time does not permit my going into the evidence in detail.

Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Woodsworth
Several illustrations of corporate practice were given. The first case was that of the Robert Simpson Company, and in this connection the report states:
In creating the security-structure an additional burden of fixed cost of $1,000,000 per annum, was placed on the operating company.
The report refers to two appraisals of the fixed assets of the Canadian Appraisal Company, by virtue of which over $8,000,000 was written into the capital. These are not my *words, these are not vague speculations, they are conclusions arrived at by the commission from the evidence. There was the Burns case involving a write-up of assets for the purpose of establishing a nominal asset value to cover the value of new securities, in other words, stock watering. The report states that this represents a distinctly doubtful case of an investment house misstating the income figures. The report questions the propriety of a refinancing, utilizing these practices at the height of a business boom. It says, referring to this practice:
One of the most flagrant which we have encountered. We wish to condemn without reservation or equivocation such financial malpractice as it illustrates.
If a man steals a loaf of bread he is liable to be sent to gaol, but it is quite possible that a man may steal from the public a million dollars and be regarded as one of the pillars of society. I submit that it is the responsibility of this government to place upon the criminal code such provisions as will enable the public to punish those who have so defrauded society and to seek the restitution of their ill gotten gains.
Another instance was given, that of Canadian Canners, and the reorganization of the company's plant, revaluation and appreciation -at least $6,000,000, equivalent to over 50 per cent of the outstanding capital stock. This is what is said, and I would call this to the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) if he would do me the courtesy of caring for any of these matters. May I ask that he be prepared to consider rather carefully some of these statements, which it seems to me affect fundamentally the administration of justice in this country. With regard to Canadian Canners, the report speaks of an inaccurate statement-a very mild term-of the company's financial position. It declares:
An inaccurate statement of the company's financial position was shown by the balance sheet presented to the shareholders in 1932; this was signed by the company's auditors, only subject to certain vital qualifications. The profits as shown did not in fact exist.
We have all heard of men who were carried off to gaol for selling some little article under
false pretences; we know of men who have been imprisoned for having forged a cheque for a few dollars; and yet here are men in responsible positions, belonging to an organization that is supposed to be above reproach, responsible for the signing of statements in which we are told that the profits as shown did not in fact exist. Take this summary of the situation-again I quote from the report:
Vendors and promoters allot shares to themselves for services and properties contributed to the company at a figure grossly in excess of
any possible intrinsic value	The courts
will force a man who has paid $99 for a $100 par share to contribute the other dollar; they seldom do anything about the man who has contributed a table worth possibly $10 at the absurd valuation of $20,000.
This is not a matter that affects only the individuals immediately concerned; it is a load on the whole consuming, the whole general public, who directly or indirectly must pay a tax because of such practices. In any case, I submit that it is the public that pays. One law for the rich and one for the poor; that has again and again been denied in this house; but I submit that we do not need to go outside the covers of this report for the most adequate evidence that that in fact really obtains.
A few years ago we had a very careful investigation, two or three in fact, into the Beauhamois scandal; but these investigations led to no punishment whatever. They led to no restitution to the public of properties that had been obtained in a scandalous manner, and now we are being besieged by second bondholders who are urging that they have been left holding the bag.
To no small extent does this irresponsible oligarchy control government policy. To the truth of our statement the statute books give the most eloquent testimony. It was only the other day that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) asserted very emphatically that it was not true that property rights took priority over human welfare. I have not time to argue the point in detail, but I suggest that all anyone has to do is to look over our statute books and over Hansard to see the reception which various resolutions and bills have met with, to my knowledge at any rate, in the last fifteen years. You have only to do that to find that property rights are very well guarded indeed but that in a great many instances human rights are callously disregarded.
The situation in Canada is not the result of socialistic experiment. Any of us who advocate anything new along this line are told that it would plunge the country into chaos. I say that the situation we face to-
446	COMMONS
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Woodsworth
day is decidedly not the result of any socialistic experiments; it is the result of years of capitalist domination. The big business men of this country have had a free hand. I think it is really a curious thing that to-day these big business men come along and tell us that we must not experiment, and try to blame the public for a situation for which they themselves are very largely responsible.
I have tried to point out that we have a small oligarchy that controls the economic situation. I think that is clear from the evidence, and I go further and assert that this system has failed to provide security and a decent standard of living for large numbers of our people. What about the primary producer? I give the results of an investigation that I myself made on the basis of the census figures of 1931. In the census year there were 728,623 farms in Canada and the average income per farm would be slightly less than $700. This figure would include cash income and value of products raised on the farm for consumption by the farm population.	The value of the farm income,
which was already small enough in 1930, had been reduced by one-quarter by 1932. It means that the average farmer to-day receives an income of only around $500 a year. Is that a satisfactory condition for our agricultural producers? The report states:
It is clear that the fundamental problem of the primary producer is finding profitable markets. The difficulty is not that he cannot produce enough goods. Nor is it that, having regard to potential demand and consumption, he produces too much: neither is it that his products are not needed and desired. It is simply that they cannot be sold at a price sufficiently high _ to maintain a reasonable standard of living for the producer nor, paradoxically, bought at a price sufficiently low to permit necessary consumption by ail in need.... At the same time, free competition in the international market is checked on every hand' by tariffs, quotas, exchange, restrictions and embargoes. The primary producer is therefore denied the possible benefits of free competition in the buying markets of the world; is exposed to all the rigours of free competition in production at home; and finally, is subjected to exploitation by outright monopoly or imperfect competition among the domestic purchasers of his product.
... Between the farmer and the consumer there is an immense gap bridged by a chain o-f middlemen each of whom exacts a proportion of the consumer's dollar. In many instances the amount received by the farmer for his product is only a fraction of that realized by this array of middlemen.
I should like to ask what the Liberal government propose to do about this situation. As a matter of fact very few members of the government are in their seats at present; I see the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers),
fMr. Woodsworth.]
the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) and a few others. I should like to ask them what the government propose to do about this situation which bears so hardly upon the producer. I turn to the Minister of Labour; what about labour? Let me point out to the minister that two-thirds of the working population of Canada are wage-earners; that is, 2,565,000 out of the whole working population of 3,923,000. If agriculture, in which over 1,000,000 people are engaged, chiefly as proprietors, were . eliminated the proportion would be increased to nearly five-sixths. The report points out that each employer starts his negotiation of the labour contract with the bargaining advantage of a mass buyer.
I am not going to plead the cause of trade unionism here, but what about the conditions of labour in Canada to-day? Take the needle trades. I ran hurriedly over the various industries as to which we have evidence in this report. In the needle trades I find that in some Quebec country home-work contract shops the workers receive only five cents per hour. Wage rates are very low; hours are very long. I quote this phrase:
Frank exploitation of labour's weakness has been common.... There are frequent and continuous violations of the laws about employment conditions, hours and wages. Female operatives were sometimes forced to work at such high pressure for continuous hours that the result on health and morals was deplorable.
This is the conclusion:
That labour and wage conditions in this branch-
That is, the needle trades.
-of Canada's industrial activity are such as to merit the most emphatic condemnation. They should not be tolerated in any state that claims to call itself civilized.
I would suggest that the Minister of Labour has a pretty big job on his hands when that statement is made in the report of the price spreads committee, with regard to conditions in this country.
The worker in the clothing industry can expect neither comfort nor security; in many cases, he can, indeed, expect only hopeless poverty.	-
What about the rights of citizenship? We have always taken it for granted that we did not need any laws on our statute books to protect certain rights of citizenship; we thought they were inherent, but these people have no rights, not even the common right of earning a decent livelihood. And what about those employed in the leather and boot industry? In 1931 the average annual

Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Woodsworth
wage was $764, while female workers earned from thirteen to twenty ^six cents per hour. Then there is furniture; I am just taking casual sentences. The average weekly earnings in each furniture factory ranged from $3.64 to $14.42, and averaged about $10. So it is with baking, with flour milling. In connection with meat packing, I have underlined this sentence:
The lowest average weekly wages found were $15.89, paid in the Hull plant of Canada Packers. In this plant 39-2 per cent of the employees were paid below the legal minimum for women in Ontario.
Here is another sentence, with regard to fruit and vegetable canning:
-both male and female time workers were paid as low as ten cents an hour.
Then we have the tobacco industry, to which I think so much publicity was given that I need not say very much about it to-day. The report states:
The most striking fact revealed by our evidence on the tobacco industry is the combination of low wages and high profits.
We all know from the press how low were those wages and how exorbitantly high were those profits. Then what about textiles? I quote:
-the average wage rate for all male workers was ten cents per hour-
The report was speaking of M. E. Binz Company, Limited. Then a word with regard to the food chains:
-In the Quebec division three companies had fifty per cent or more of the male grocery clerks receiving less than $10 per week, but three companies had also twenty-five per cent or more of their female employees in this class- hours of labour of employees of food chains are longer than any worker should be asked to endure

Let me call that sentence to the attention of the Minister of Labour and ask him what he proposes to do about it. I have spoken about the situation of the producer and the situation of the labour man. What is the situation of the small business man? In approximately one-third of the retail business of this country the personal factor has largely disappeared; that is the social side.
Economically, the unwarranted expansion in recent years in distributive, as in industrial organizations, has not contributed to the general welfare

What about the consumer? Well, frankly the consumer-and let me point out that we are all consumers-has been cheated all along the line.
-such practices include: false and misleading advertising and marking; misleading statements as to quality of products, including designation of grades of goods likely to confuse or deceive
rather than inform the consumer-short weight and unjust scales-
Again I ask the. Minister of Justice what his department is going to do with regard to wholesale cheating of this kind. Surely that is just as much a criminal offence as anything we have prohibited by statute. Then let us look at the milling interests; although the Minister of Finance is not present I think perhaps he ought to give this house some indication as to what can be done in that industry. In this report the statement is made that the public and not the industry has been bearing the burden of its cost. Take bread; there has been an increase in the spread between flour and bread prices from 2-33 cents per pound in 1916 to 5-13 cents per pound in 1930, which is equal to 4-2 cents per one and one-half pound loaf. Whether we look at it from the standpoint of the producer, the business man, the labour man or the consumer, here we have a situation that is very unsatisfactory, to say the least.
What can be done about that situation? Last year the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) attempted to do something. Most of his legislation seems in a fair way to be put on the scrap heap. What are the Liberals going to do? They are now the government in power. The older economic theories of the Liberals, I think, were fairly well expressed by Mr. E. J. Young, who formerly represented the constituency of Weybum. What did he say with regard to monopolies:
The only effective way to deal with monopolistic organizations is to expose them to merciless competition, which will force them to efficiency or to bankruptcy-
Surely the Liberals ought to understand that it is owing to merciless competition that we have arrived at the state in which we find ourselves to-day. It is by merciless competition that the big fellows have been able to drive the little fellows to the wall.
With regard to export trade-and I think this is a matter that the Liberals will have to consider seriously-this is what Mr. Young said:
In order to dispose of our exports, we must sell them at prices the people of other countries can pay.
To do this, it is necessary to keep our production costs down to a point that will enable us to compete in the markets of the world, with other countries producing similar products.
Are we then to reduce our production costs by driving labour still lower? I ask the Liberals in all seriousness, is that their only solution? I am glad to think that the great Liberal party is gradually getting away from that old laissez-faire policy.
448	COMMONS
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Woodsworth
Here are some lines that I found not long
ago in the Manchester Guardian. The poem -if it can be called such-was entitled, Lancashire:
.... then came steam
Machines that marched the floor with the measured precision of the planetary system,
And towns that sprawled in muddles of beastliness:
Had hands tender as a lover's for yarn and hard as Cain's for the children they enslaved.
See the woman weaving in that steam-heated shed?
There's a kid coming.
But the Act says she mustn't go on weaving after... .
Oh, it does, does it?
And the Act says the humidity mustn't exceed....
Oh, it does, does it?
Mustn't exceed warm tea. She's stood eight hours:
Is she tired? Oh boy?
They've found how to save the cotton trade;
London chap, he found it. He spent a whole day in Manchester.
Lancashire must reduce her costs and recover the export trade.
Exactly the position stated in the dissenting report of the former member for Weybum. The lines go on:
Lancashire must-Oh, my God.
I know an economist lives in a library and studies trade.
It's the best place. Inside a library you see all trade, and outside you only see part, the part that hurts,
Demand he said, is satisfied from the cheapest supply.
Productive energies which no longer conform to this condition should be transferred to alternative activities.
What sheltered lives these long words lead! Never been soaked with sweat or cold with fear. Never been parts of men, like short words.
Productive energies which no longer-that's me and my mill. Are you getting it?
That is the attitude of finance. I am not accusing the Liberals of callous disregard of human suffering, but I say to them that in view of the deplorable conditions that exist to-day, whatever their theories, this country expects them to take some immediate action to solve these outstanding problems. I think most of them, and I hope most hon. members of this house, will agree with the conclusions of the price spreads commission in this report:
The depression has, furthermore, demonstrated that the strong and the organized are attaining an ever increasing position of dominance in our economic life; that economic power is becoming concentrated. With this concentration, old theories of economic control are proving inadequate.

.	.	. Unregulated competition no longer
guarantees efficiency and maximum production at fair prices. Competition degenerates sometimes into economic warfare where victory may go to the strong, rather than to the efficient. Forces of economic readjustment are often not self-correcting, but cumulative in their efforts. Orderly readjustments may develop into disorderly crises.
I congratulate the Liberals upon having put into the speech from the throne the statement that appears there with regard to the necessity of state intervention under certain circumstances. That is all to the good.
It is most unfortunate that there was no one on the price spreads commission who stressed public ownership and operation. Indeed the commission definitely expressed a prejudice against it. But they did say:
Under present conditions, then, the question is not intervention or non-intervention, but merely the nature and extent of intervention.
I wish we could have had that clearly recognized; we would have had much more illuminating discussions on the hustings in the last election. The report extending over some pages covers various forms of state control, I have time only to enumerate them;
(a)	Protection of private economic activity;
(b)	promotion of private economic activity;
(c)	the encouragement of monopoly; (d) licensing; (e) protection of the public; (f) prohibition of monopoly; (g) government acceptance of monopoly; (h) government toleration of monopolistic or quasi-monopolistic industrial combinations, such as cartels, and, (i) public ownership and operation. It is this last which ia treated so very slightly in the commission's report, but which we believe ought to form a line of policy for this country. This is what the report said:
The extreme example of government intervention is where the government engages directly in the ownership and operation of business enterprise. Government ownership and operation of postal services, schools, and roads provide some of the oldest examples. In violation of extreme individualistic theories, governments nearly everywhere have taken these enterprises out of private hands, sometimes simply because private enterprise could not profitably supply satisfactory service, sometimes because it did not operate to produce maximum social welfare. Public ownership for^ a variety of reasons-to provide a competitive check on private enterprise, to supplement ineffective regulations of monopoly, to control consumption, to provide revenue- has continued to expand until a world survey of such ownership to-day would include every type of economic activity. In Canada governments are directly engaged in such businesses as railways, steamships, street railways, telegraphs, telephones, radio, electric light and' power, water, gas, stockyards, grain elevators, public markets, liquor sales, banking, and insurance.

Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. MacNicol
Under these circumstances I submit that we of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party are quite within our rights and indeed in the line of progress in urging that the government itself should take over many of these enterprises. The question is not individual enterprise versus bureaucratic monopoly, but rather whether the inevitable monopoly shall be irresponsible and inefficient as at present, or fascist in type, or democratic. We plead for democratic control in industry. I know that in Canada there is some difficulty in working out our policy owing to the division of powers under the British North America Act as between the provincial and the federal authorities, but I submit that we as a federal parliament could do a great deal more under the British North America Act than we are doing at present. Hon. members will remember the clause by which complete control is given the dominion over- -such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces. (92, 10c.)
I think the hon. member for East Kootenay is right in saying that very much more could be done than is being done under that act. Then I urge further, and I trust that some of my colleagues will develop this point, that within the framework of state control there should be the fullest opportunities for cooperative enterprises, both consumers' and producers' cooperatives: I should like also to have emphasized that it is not the goods that we need socialized, but the capacity to produce.
Under a cooperative commonwealth, instead of profits for a few we would give service to the many, to the whole community. We would seek to establish democracy in our every day living. Remember that five-sixths of the non-agricultural working population consists of wage earners. To-day they have no control of the very means by which they live. Can that condition be called democracy?
Especially in view of the international situation, caused we believe to a great extent by the economic forces at work in the world, we urge that it is desirable that we substitute for our highly competitive system one based on cooperation. I wish every hon. member could be induced to read a recent book by H. N. Brailsford entitled, Property or Peace. I firmly believe a fundamental change in our economic system is the only 12739-29
way to bring about lasting peace. Permanent peace can be assured only when the underlying principles of cooperation replace those of competition.

I agree with the hon. member's observations about the farmers, to the effect that their incomes are too low. On the other hand I disagree with his statements about industry. I know of many industries which during the last four or five years have been operating without a profit and, on the contrary, have suffered great losses. The proletarian government must withdraw all state support from the church, which is the agency of the former ruling classy it must prevent all church interference in state-organized educational affairs, and ruthlessly suppress the counter-revolutionary activity of the ecclesiastical organizations.
Then on page 67:
The mighty social power of the imperialist state, with its auxiliary apparatus-schools, press, theatre and church-is primarily reflected in the existence of confessional and reformist tendencies among the working class, which represent the main obstacles on the road towards the proletarian social revolution. The confessional, religiously tinged tendency among the working class, finds expression in the confessional trade unions, which frequently are directly connected with corresponding bourgeois political organizations and are affiliated to one or other of the church organizations of the dominant class (Catholic trade unions', Young Men's Christian Association, Jewish Zionist organizations, etc.). All these tendencies. being the most striking product of the ideological captivity of certain strata of the proletariat, in most cases, bear a romantic feudal tinge. By sanctifying all the abominations of the capitalist regime with the holy water of religion, and by terrorizing^ their flock with the spectre of punishment in the *world to come, the leaders of these organizations serve as the most reactionary units of the class enemy in the camp of the proletariat.
Now I care not what its denomination may be, the church that is honest in its convictions -and I believe they all have been-has done a great work throughout history, and when I find an organization designed to destroy the church in all countries I am opposed to it. As I said at the outset, I do not believe that my friends to the left are communists, nor do I believe they would advocate violence. On the other hand let me repeat that they cannot continue to talk as they have been talking, stirring up the masses in this country, without causing trouble.
I know a great many things are wrong, and I will support anything that will help make them right. The hon. gentleman mentioned a number of changes that I would support, but revolution is not the way to bring about reform, nor can it be brought about through the destruction of the capitalistic system. I may tell my hon. friends that it is not the capitalistic system that has caused the trouble; it is the violations of the capitalistic system, and these can be wiped out by law. I have no fault to find with the true principles of the capitalistic system; time does not permit me to enumerate them, but they are worthy. I would be prepared to go a long way in order to stop the practices referred to by the hon. gentleman, those violations of the capitalistic system, but I am not prepared to destroy the
whole system because some rascals have exploited the public when they should not have been allowed to do so.
I am glad to know that there has been some measure of reform attained in connection with many of the vile stock-market practices to which the hon. gentleman referred. I am ready to support unemployment insurance; I have supported it, and I believe it should be introduced in this ocuntry. I suppose I should not mention it to-day, but I hope that when the supreme court gives its judgment it will be in favour of the principle of unemployment insurance. I would break up the dishonest trusts mentioned by the hon. gentleman. There may be an occasional trust that is financially sound, but I would break up the great trusts that are throttling the workers, and return them to their component parts. I would lower interest rates; they have been too high, but that is not the fault of the capitalistic system. That is something that has been permitted by law, but the law can eradicate that. Then I would do something to save the homes of the workers in the cities, just as we have taken steps to save the farms. I would shorten hours; I would improve working conditions and I would abolish sweat shops. These were permitted under the capitalistic system, but they constitute a violation of that system that never should have been permitted. I would also protect the interests of small business men, to whom the hon. gentleman referred. I agree with him when he says small business has been throttled, but it can be protected by law.
The hon. gentleman mentioned something about the consumers. In England I have read they have a consumers' council, and any one who buys goods for which he thinks he has been overcharged can go before the public prosecutor representing the consumers' council and register his complaint. I would go so far as to advocate something of that nature in this country, so that people who feel that they have been gypped can appeal to a public prosecutor, who will take steps to prosecute whoever has gypped them. I have no doubt that may people are gypped on prices.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would make every effort possible to provide work for the working men. In my time I have had a lot to do with work. I have heard men talk about labour who I know have never had a thing to do with labour. I have had to do with many thousands of working men in my time, and I am only too willing to do everything possible to raise their standards, alleviate their trials and provide work for them. Many men wlio talk about labour and industry cannot, from

Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that this is a thought-provoking resolution, and in some ways it was well presented by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). The only feature one might deplore in that presentation is the fact that

at times a certain amount of bitterness appeared to be displayed, and I do not believe that is conducive to a really national and constructive spirit in dealing with the very important problems which have to be faced at the moment.
I well remember that during the last campaign our good friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation had a great big motto. They depicted the fifty big shots of this dominion, and with hatred and bitterness they tried to spread all through the north, if not through the whole of Canada, the thought that the so-called wealthy men were being absolutely unfair not only to the people but also to the country that had allowed them to amass their wealth. I do not think that sort of thing helps the national situation. I also remember that my Cooperative Commonwealth Federation opponent, who by the way was a personal friend of mine, strongly criticized me because I had the audacity to meet and shake hands for the first time with Mr. Noah Timmins, the genial head of the Hollinger mines. That was the first time I met Mr. Timmins; it was also the last time, because since then he has gone to his reward. At that time I did not think that criticism was worthy of the cooperative commonwealth party.
We should realize that we must be fair not only to all sections of our people but also to the so-called big interests for some of them certainly play the game. Just at this point I should like to allude to a booklet that was issued by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, again dealing with the so-called fifty big shots. I must tell my hon. friend the leader of that party that personally I have never had an opportunity of meeting any of these big shots, but judging by the booklet members of his party must have fraternized with them a good deal for they want to create the impression that they know them. In this booklet, which is entitled Who Owns Canada, at page 12 the fifty big shots are enumerated, with their names, their places of birth, their ages, their professions, their religious denominations, their education, their bank directorships and the total assets of the corporations with which they are connected. If my addition is not in error, according to this statement these fifty big shots control some S97,000,000,000 of wealth. It seems incredible that any such statement should be made by a party supposed to be working for universal suffrage and hoping to be given the political leadership of this country.

Cooperative Commonwealth

Mr. Bradette
Everyone who is familiar with the economic affairs of this dominion or who follows the publications of the bureau of statistics realizes that our national wealth does not amount to $25,000,000,000 but in this booklet just for the sake of exaggeration these fifty big shots are said to command $97,000,000,000. Such statements are absolutely unfair, and the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation has overstepped the mark in bringing out that old war horse during the last by-election campaign in Assiniboia, accusing the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) of being in the pay of the Standard Oil and under the guidance of the so-called big shots when he went to Washington during the great war. That statement is libellous and they know it. A discussion of this nature is bound to do some good as long as we keep within the confines of truth, but wild statements such as these will not bring about a realization of all our dreams and a solution of our deep and multiple problems. Everyone wants prosperity and happiness; we want to do away with sharp practices, dishonesty and all the other evils that were revealed by the price spreads commission, and the present government has fully grasped the situation and is going to take action to correct the shortcomings shown by that commission as far as our commerce, finance and industry are concerned.
It is not my intention to single out any industry, but an allusion was made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to the sorry plight of the retail trade. I can speak of that with knowledge because I happen to belong to that calling. No doubt we have sinned ourselves. Take my own case; when we turned our business into a limited company we had $65,000 on our own books as credit extended to our customers. Most of them are honest. On the other hand in many cases customers do not want to pay for goods they have received. I must state here that we saw that none of our customers ever went hungry. Sharp practices are not confined to any class of the population. It is an impressive ceremony when we open every sitting of the house with the Lord's prayer. I believe in the full application of that divine prayer lies the solution of all our problems. In a former session the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) mentioned the great lessons to be learned from the sermon on the mount, and the great fundamental principles that were then enunciated are just as alive to-day as they were then. It is doubtless true that the wealthy people of this country have sinned against the
present social order, but it might do some good to look at matters fairly and recognize that the so-called other classes of people have at times sinned also.
I have listened many times to hon. members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group building up a case on behalf of a cooperative commonwealth federation by singling out a particular case of misery and want, but I also could build up a case, showing that some of the misery is not always caused by the present social order. During last Easter recess I happened to be at my home on Good Friday and a settler whom I have known for a number of years came to me and said, "Joe, I have already received $30 direct relief in April, but it is all gone and I need $30 more to carry me through the month, because I have a wife and seven children. I telephoned the relief officer and he gave this man another $30. This was Good Friday. On Saturay night this father of a family was in gaol; every cent of that money given to help his wife and children was Bpent by himself for liquor. It is all very well to make a case against the so-called big shots and to single them out, but we have to live under the present order. I know I am on dangerous ground when making such a statement, and it might not be very popular, but duty compels me to tell the truth. All classes of our people have to some extent sinned and in some degree are responsible for the present situation.
My hon. friends want to bring about a new order. During the last election campaign I was interrupted by a Cooperative Commonwealth Federation adherent. I said to him, "What are you going to do while you are building up your new order? You want to destroy the present capitalistic system and put in a better one." He said, "Yes, we are going to have a working man's government." But when a man is elected to parliament, whether he is a minister or a professional man or a farmer or a mechanic, no matter what occupation he may have been engaged in, he has to leave it for months if not for a number of years while he occupies his seat in the House of Commons, so surely in this chamber we are all, in the full sense of the term, working men. We all want to see the present anomalies and injustices-and they are very numerous- done away with. I do not hold any brief for the capitalistic system or for any individual capitalists, but this system is not the result of pure hazard; it has not been built up over night it has developed out of the experience of human beings during the centuries, yes, for thousands of years. It reflects
458	COMMONS
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Bradette
the aspirations, the passions, the vices, the infirmities and, indeed all the qualities of humankind. No one doubts that it needs reform, but no one will dare to say that nationalization of all our social and economic and industrial activity is the simple formula that will solve all our problems. These problems are not peculiar to Canada; they affect the whole civilized world.
Let me refer for a moment to one line of activity that is supposed to be nationalized in Ontario. I do not say this in a disparaging way. Is nationalization always fair to the people? I say no. Ontario has had public ownership of hydro for nearly thirty years, but in northern Ontario, although we have contributed a large share to the provincial treasury to help the hydro commission in the southern section of the province, we have to depend upon private capital and private enterprise for the development of the great water powers of our northern section, and even to-day new mines do not get their power from the Ontario Hydro Electric Commission but the risk has to be taken by private enterprise. IV e in northern Ontario have paid to some extent-and we are supposed to be glad to do so-towards the millions of dollars supplied by the provincial treasury to bonus rural lines to the well-to-do farmers and to furnish power to the industries in the southern section of the province. I mention this in order that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre may see that even nationalization is not always fair to ail sections of the population.
The same state of affairs is shown by the present radio situation. When the bill for national control of radio was brought in I voted for it with both hands because I believed then and believe now that great national service should belong to the people. Perhaps I was selfish to some extent, because I realized that in the larger centres of population like Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, etcetera, they were getting good radio service under private ownership, and I am sorry to say now that under nationalization of the radio and that service will be extended to everyone-the people of northern Ontario and Quebec, although they have to pay $2 a year for a licence, are even yet not getting the service to which we are absolutely entitled.
Governments have all the infirmities and vices of human beings and very few of their good qualities. History teaches that lesson to whoever wants to read it. Some public services, such as the Department of Justice, are clearly subjects for national control; no one would think of having the administration of justice left to private initiative and enterprise. The same applies to the post office,

public health and national defence. But surely it was never intended under British institutions, with the mentality of the British nations, that the government should take control of all industrial and economic activity and the supply of all social wants; such a situation would be absolutely impracticable and is foreign to the thought of the Canadian people. We all remember what happened in England, the great revolution brought about following the middle of the last century by the invention of steam power. Can anyone visualize what would have happened if when the steam engine was invented, the British parliament had nationalized its development and had invested hundreds of millions of pounds so as to develop that new invention? Further, can anyone visualize what would have happened and what attitude the government would have taken when some time later the internal combustion engine and electric motive power were invented? Do hon. members think for one moment that the government would have been elastic enough, after having invested hundreds of millions of dollars in the steam engine, to throw that money away, scrap all its antiquated machinery and take on the development of the later invention, as private enterprise has done? No, because such matters are governmentally and humanly impossible. I suggest these are points worth remembering when we are discussing matters of this kind.
I well remember that during the session of 1934, in a discussion of the bullion tax mentioned in the budget, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre rose in his place and suggested that we should nationalize gold mining in Canada. I asked him some questions when, later on, I spoke on the budget debate. First I asked him what gold mining he was going to nationalize, those on a dividend basis or those not on a dividend basis. What about new ventures? What about prospecting? What about new finds?
I remember well what happened in Ontario in the great silver camp at Cobalt years ago when the provincial government decided to try to control one of the silver mines. That effort was one of the greatest failures we have known, and I believe the principle applying in that instance would apply to any government going beyond its proper activities.
The work of a government is not creative; in my opinion its duties and powers are legislative. Can any hon. member visualize governments, wherever they may be, in the provinces or here at Ottawa, inventing developments of steam engines or radio? Can anyone visualize a government creating and bringing up to its present perfection the great
FEBRUARY 24, 1936	[DOT]	459
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Bradette
automotive industry in Canada? No; the primary duty of a government is to take accomplished facts, and on those facts to build up and to legislate for the happiness and prosperity of the nation it governs. The minute we establish a bureaucracy-and I am using the word in its full sense-and the moment we have full authority in all matters, economic, industrial, social and financial, then what will become of the individualism of. the British people? I say that we shall become merely automatons.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has often pointed to the great prosperity of Russia. He must know the horrible price the Russians have paid for that measure of prosperity. The trouble has been that some of their reforms have been made too quickly; the people of that country have been too impatient, too ruthless. When I hear of a bacteriologist dealing with bacteria and germs in carrying out his experiments and learn that those germs are killed by the millions and billions I do not worry very much and I am inclined to believe they rather like it. When I hear that a biologist is experimenting on dogs and sheep and learn that those animals have lost their lives in the process of experimentation then I begin to worry a great deal. But when I see new experiments on new social systems, w'hen I find that those performing the experiments, those using the knives of vivisection, are using them not on dogs or sheep or germs, but on human beings, and when I see the state of affairs in Spain, Germany and Russia, where hundreds of thousands of human lives have been lost in these new social experiments, I begin to shiver, and highly protest against such experiences.
In beginning my observations to-day I said some good could come from a discussion of this subject. In these times no one is in a position to stand on a pinnacle and say: Because I am wealthy and because this world has been good to me I am away from all the backwaters and the turmoil of the depression. That man must come down into the valley and see what the people are suffering, what are their aspirations, what they expect. The same principle applies to the people living in the valley. To some extent and in some way all of us must realize that we have a duty to perform towards ourselves and towards the state. Unfortunately however those great problems will never be solved by extreme radicalism, advanced socialism or communism, because, as the previous speaker (Mr. MacNicol) has said, no matter how much the Cooperative Commonwealth
Federation tries to divorce itself from the communist party it cannot do so. I watched the operations of that party in the Kirkland lake section during the last campaign, and I came to the one logical conclusion, namely, that socialization has only one result and that result is a state of communism.
As I stated before, the time is not ripe, and I hope will never be, to have socialism in Canada. Some great duties have to be performed. Only a few days ago I listened with a great deal of interest to a good speech delivered by Sir Edward Beatty in which he stated that the business men of Canada must be ready and willing to sacrifice, to realize fully their duty and obligations; they must listen to the murmurs of the people, attempt to cooperate with them to the greatest extent . and come down from their high estate.
During the last five years every section of our population has been seriously affected by the depression. During the first two years, however, some people thought they were specially privileged. But the longer the depression lasted the more pronounced was the decrease in the number of privileged ones. The question before us is not so much that of the destruction of personal initiative nor that of the equalization of wealth, but rather one of a better distribution of wealth and the application of those economic and Christian principles whereby we may do away with poverty. No one can be spared from the strenuousness of the present times. There used to be a time when it was considered that poverty was a necessity, but to-day under a capitalistic system and due to human inventiveness poverty could be destroyed throughout the world. What we want to do is to bring it to the point where the so-called common people will have full rights of citizenship and access to the good things in life, with drastic changes in our present distribution system.
I have no time this afternoon to propound certain theories that I have in mind, but again I appeal to the house that in a discussion of a resolution such as this we must try to remain within the truth, and not endeavour to set one section of the country against another. I believe the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation wants to be fair, but is he acting like a true Canadian when he tries to impute to every wealthy man in Canada an unfair attitude towards those less fortunate? That is not always the case. A few days ago the hon. member for East Kootenay (Mr. Stevens) referred to reforms
460	COMMONS
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Bradette
which had been accomplished by one of the larger corporations of the city of Montreal. He indicated that they had made amendments to their method of procedure with effects beneficial not only to their own customers but to themselves.
I can well remember when three years ago in northern Ontario we had a lumbermen's and buishmen's strike. On that occasion I went to the manager of a big corporation and said, "You are not playing the game with the men who are working for you; you are not giving them fair wages; you are not giving them decent living quarters; you are selling your goods at too high a price, and I must remind you that you are not in the retail trade, but in the lumber business. You should sell your goods to your working men at least at cost." A year ago last fall we had some trouble again in the Cochrane and Iroquois Falls section. I went to one point at which a strike had been called and to which strike breakers had been sent. Upon that occasion I found that the men had been given a decent living; that they had a reading room; that they were satisfied with the food, and that they had an opportunity at least once a week to state through their own organizations their grievances before the heads of the company. You could not take those men away. Some of them had been working for that company for two years, were absolutely satisfied with their lot and would not go on strike.
This is not the time for those corporations to make enormous profits, but it is time for those men in elevated positions to come down from their high pedestals and attempt to underetand the Canadian people and find out what their aspirations may be. I must repeat however that the solution will never, never be found in rash measures. It will never be found in a policy which makes automatons of the Canadian people. Can we visualize the advancement of the British empire if government had been supreme in matters of private interest? It is true that at the present time we have sufficient machinery to do the work we require to do, and if we apply it properly, do away with all sharp practices. The hon. member for East Kootenay stated that the price spreads inquiry disclosed that some concerns were selling their products on short weights. There are laws as old as the hills on the statute books of Canada and on those of all civilized countries stating that giving short weight is contrary to law. It is a criminal offence, and there is certainly nothing new about it. We are not so much

in need of new laws to place on our statute books, so far as that point is concerned, as of the fuller application of the laws we have. Certainly we have sufficient machinery to make these people act fairly, and we must deal with them more drastically and make them more aware of their duty to the public.
May I repeat that I believe some thanks ought to be given to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for affording this opportunity to members of parliament to deal with problems facing us at the present time. Faced with these great problems some people would tell us that we should not even smile, but we must smile, Mr. Speaker, even in times of stress because we are struggling towards something better. These are times to cultivate courage and fortitude. Even during the war humanity found it possible to go forward. There is no doubt that we have been suffering along with the other peoples of the world, but we are seized of the exact situation and are endeavouring to go to the root of the trouble. We must not be impatient, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre must remember that if a new socialistic state were erected in Canada to-morrow he would still have our present day problems on his hands and they cannot be solved overnight or by a miracle. Spain became impatient a few years ago and turned to a socialistic experiment. So did France over a century ago when the slogan was equality, liberty and fraternity. What kind of fraternity had they? The fraternity of the guillotine. What kind of equality had they? The equality of the graveyard, and conscription in the army. And so far as freedom is concerned their armies had to face the rest of Europe. About the same thing happened in Russia.
I listened very attentively to the address of the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. He said that if' he were in power he would not socialize the land, but, Mr. Speaker, if you socialize industry, the financial institutions and the economic life of the country, there is only one thing that the farmers will get, and that is the nationalization of the land; you cannot get away from it. That is what happened in Russia, and that point is worth considering.
I do not doubt the sincerity of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He has done a lot of good in many ways; he has blazed the trail in some directions, but sometimes one can overstep the mark and undo the good work that has been done in the past, I have no advice to give him because he has had

Cooperative Commonwealth-Miss Macphail
a larger experience than I have, but I would say that to pit one class against another is not conducive to a healthy national situation in our country. Rather do I believe in the adherence of mutual respect and closer cooperation on the part of all classes and all walks of life, young and old, wealthy and poor, because the goal to reach, although hard, is worthy of attainment.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Grey-Bruce): Mr. Speaker, reading over the resolution standing on the order paper in the name of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), I find it says:
That, in the opinion of this house, industrial, commercial and financial organizations and undertakings that are failing to function in the general interest should be taken over by the appropriate public authorities and operated as public services or cooperative enterprises.
I do not see anything very alarming in that wording. I am always interested in the eloquence of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Bradette) but I would suggest that he do not exercise himself unduly over the radicalism of this resolution. It seems to me a very sensible and certainly not too radical resolution, and I want to address myself more particularly to the latter portion of it relating to cooperative enterprises.
These resolutions spring upon one, and I am more and more coming to the conclusion that the only way to be able to speak to them is to have a lot of speeches already prepared and put away in cold storage. I have not got around to doing that, and so I cannot make in any sense a prepared speech. But increasingly I am coming to believe in the cooperative approach to the solution of many of our Canadian problems.
For a long time we have heard with a great deal of interest of the success of cooperative producers' societies in Denmark and Sweden, and of cooperative consumers' societies in Great Britain, but it is only recently that we have found in Canada examples that promise to have the strength and inspiration of the Danish and British experiments. We have in this country a very interesting organization called the Cooperative Union, which seeks to bind together all the consumer cooperatives and to carry on educational work among them. In their publication of January this year I find this statement on the front page, which puts
the aim of the cooperative movement better than I could unaided:
We must seek to show that all our institutions. no matter how splendid and no matter how proud we may be of having played a part in their creation, are merely a means to an end. The end is the freeing of men and women from economic and social thraldom.
That is putting it very well. Everyone must admit that our economic system has caused economic and social slavery, and I do not think anyone in the house would care to defend the conditions we have at the moment when we see on the one hand great wealth, and on the other extreme poverty which is causing decay and degradation. Even those who are most keen for the capitalistic system-and I am not one of them -must pause before they eulogize it as it has been working out these last few years.
Now I want to speak for a moment on the cooperative movement in Denmark and of their educational system launched by such well known men as Grundtvig and Ivold. Only last week a leader in the Folk School movement, Doctor Peter Mannicke, visited this city. I am sorry to say that in the capital of Canada he had an audience of little more than two hundred people to hear his inspirational address. Nevertheless the Danes have done tremendous things in awakening the spirit of their people to unselfish and idealistic living. Our new governor general made a speech at Upper Canada College in Toronto the day before yesterday, in which he used these words, " A college should not only turn out gentlemen but aristocrats," and he defined an aristocrat as one who seeks to give more to life than he takes from it. The Danes have been doing that for a long time. They have been turning out aristocrats until to-day they might almost be said to be a nation of aristocrats in the sense that they seek to give to life more than they take from it. And the bread they have cast upon the waters has returned to them one hundredfold. They have built up their country to the point where it evokes our admiration.
The story of Denmark is quite familiar, but I think it would not hurt to take a moment to say that they have in that country 1,388 cooperative dairies, representing ninety per cent of the farms and eighty-six per cent of the cows, and the turnover in 1932 was 8116,000,000. They own and control sixty-one cooperative bacon factories representing seventy per cent of the farms and seventy-five per cent of the hogs, and in 1932 the turnover was $95,000,000. They have 700 cooperative egg-collecting stations, representing twenty per cent of the farms and twenty-five per cent

Cooperative Commonwealth-Miss Macphail
of the hens, and the turnover in 1932 was $3,500,000. One could go all the way through and mention their cooperative efforts in other commodities, their credit associations and their units of consumer cooperatives.

Miss' MACPHAIL: The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) is a very fine speaker and possibly later on, he will make his speech to which I shall enjoy listening.
Sweden has given us an example which I believe will interest hon. members. During the campaign I noticed an article which I was glad to cut out because during a time like that we are glad to read anything that is at all sane. This reads:
A considerable measure of public ownership, plus highly developed cooperative organizations, have combined to save Sweden from the worst effects of the economic crisis which is devastating purely capitalistic countries. An experiment in a managed currency, and a strong trades unionist movement, are other factors.
The article then goes on to show how the activities of these organizations had saved the people of Sweden from the worst results of the world depression. The power of the cooperative movement was shown by one instance. A great salt manufacturing establishment in Great Britain had never paid union wages to its workers in spite of the fact that the workers had striven very hard to get such wages through organization and other methods. They finally communicated their difficulty to the Swedish Cooperative Wholesale Society, which happened to be the largest

customer of the salt manufacturing establishment. The cooperative society told the manufacturing plant that if it did not agree to pay union wages to its workers they would cancel all their present orders and would give no future ones. The result was that union wages were paid. This shows that economic power is the greatest power, and this is something that all radicals should remember To give some comfort to the Minister of Finance, I might say that Sweden is now contemplating state trading in gasoline, oil and coffee.
We have heard much of the cooperatives in Great Britain. Most of us know the story of the early pioneers who started in an almost insignificant and undignified manner. To-day there is a membership of something like 7,000,000 people, a little better than one-half of the families in Great Britain belonging to cooperative societies of one kind or another. When cooperation becomes as extensive as that one can see its power. In addition to retail and wholesale consumer activities, the cooperatives in Great Britain have subsidiary activities such as banking, insurance, shipping, printing and publishing, newspapers and so on.
